catalog_quote: [p.52 fn.9] Though the penultimate and antepenultimate syllables of a word are common locations for stress cross-linguistically, Bena does not have a stress system. In a stress system, each word would must contain a stressed syllable. This means that if length were a manifestation of stress in Bena each word would have to contain a long vowel. However, in Bena it is possible to have a word that has only short syllables (for example libihi 'tree'). [p.64] Morae may be either High toned or toneless, and each word is assigned a single High tone. With only a few exceptions, word-final tone is disallowed. Odden (1988) has argued that Bena tone falls within what he refers to as "predictable tone systems." sweep_summary: Bena (bena1262, Bantu G63) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Philippson 1991 (theses.fr 1992PA05H011), was already on file (mwal1237/) and is now copied under bena1262/ and read: §2.6.1 pp. 442-444 and the synthesis card p. 508 treat Bena as an accentual language with an H* melody — two 'accent' patterns, penultimate (PB *BB/*BH stems) vs. prefix (*HB/*HH), analysed metrically with an extrametrical final syllable; he does not claim stress. The best first-hand statement is Morrison 2011 (Rice PhD, on file, text layer verified): fn. 9 p. 52 'Bena does not have a stress system', §2.3 p. 64 'each word is assigned a single High tone', §2.3.5 p. 92 'Bena's system is tonal'. Crossref abstract of Morrison 2014 and archive.org snippets of Odden 1988 agree (one predictable H per word). Not obtainable from our machine: Schumann 1917/18 ZfK 8 (not digitised on archive.org; HathiTrust/BSB/SUB-HH blocked), Eaton 2007 SIL sketch and Mitterhofer 2013 (sil.org Cloudflare), Persée PDF (altcha); Semantic Scholar, Google Books and web lookups quotas were exhausted. Recommended coding if added: no word stress; culminative predictable tone (pitch-accent type). Files and addendum:

new_statements.rule_in_words: The author states explicitly that Bena has no stress system; prominence is tonal: a restricted ('predictable') tone system with at most one High per word, whose position (penultimate mora, antepenultimate mora, stem-initial, or pre-stem-initial) is determined lexically for nouns and by tense-aspect for verbs. Phonemic and derived vowel length is confined to the penult/antepenult but is argued not to be stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final High allowed only in a few cases (possessive clitic); dialectal variation in which tone pattern (PSI/APU/PU) nouns and verb forms take; younger speakers show reduced High/Low pitch range under Swahili influence, described as possible incipient shift toward a stress-based system.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Morrison states the location of High is the same in isolation and in sentence context (p.70: 'a word pronounced in isolation has the same tone pattern as one that occurs in a sentence'). Analysis based mainly on the Ngaveta dialect (Njombe district, fieldwork 2008-2009).
new_statements.identity_note: Morrison's analysis is based mainly on the Ngaveta dialect of Bena (Njombe district); she reports dialectal variation in tone-pattern distribution across Nyikolwe, Mavemba, Twangabita, Sovi, Maswamu, Ngaveta but the no-stress/tonal characterization is given for Bena as a whole (bena1262). Not to be confused with Bena of Nigeria (Adamawa).

new_statements.reading: Bena has no word stress. Its word prosody is a restricted ('predictable') tone system: at most one High (phonetically high-falling) tone per word, positioned by rule on the penultimate, antepenultimate, pre-stem-initial or stem-initial mora depending on stem shape and tense/aspect; word-final H is nearly disallowed. Philippson 1991 (pp. 442-444, 508), read in the same sweep, gives the same picture in accentual terms ('langue accentuelle à mélodie H*': penultimate accent for etymologically low stems, prefix accent for etymologically high stems). If Bena is added to the catalog it should be coded as a culminative-tone / pitch-accent language with no stress, not as a penultimate-stress language.

sources.quote: Parmi les langues du groupe XV, seuls le kinga et le bena sont assez bien attestés. Celui-ci offre la même répartition que celle que nous avons vue dans plusieurs langues méridionales : BB et BH d'une part, HB et HH de l'autre, sont confondus en deux schèmes accentuels - en l'occurrence, accent sur la pénultième sur ceux-là, sur le préfixe pour ceux-ci. [...] synchroniquement, deux pieds sont formés dans les nominaux dont le thème comporte un H, un seul dans les autres (la syllabe finale est extra-métrique) [...] Un H est placé sur la finale de chaque pied, puis le deuxième H est dissimilé (pp. 442-443)

sources.quote: Verbal tone in Bena is characterized by a single High tone per word. Roots are toneless, and inflected forms are assigned one of four tone melodies : Pre‑Stem Initial (PSI), Macrostem Initial (MSI), Antepenultimate (APU), and Penultimate (PU). The location of H in an inflected form is entirely predictable through a combination of morphophonological criteria, including the morphological complexity of the verbal base, the tense and aspect of the verb, the form of the final suffix, and whether the verb is affirmative or negative.
sources.note: Peer-reviewed published version of the dissertation's tone chapter; may restate or refine the no-stress / culminative-H analysis and would be the citable journal source.
